{
  "entityC1": {
    "design_critique": "1) The speed change is not a new test. Speed has already been varied across the range that matters. Iteration 6 (base 0.8) and iteration 3 (base 0.9) give identical oval progress (0.1675), max_error (0.0661 to 0.0662) and line-loss counts. Iteration 5 (base 1.0) gives the same oval progress. Iterations 0 and 1 (base 1.4 to 1.6) gave oval progress of 0.115 to 0.176, within the same band. Across base speeds 0.8 to 1.6 the failure point has not moved, so the draft's claim that speed is 'the untested factor' is contradicted by its own evidence. Dropping to 0.6 is extrapolation from a flat response, not a test of a live variable. The draft should say so.

2) Progress is spatially fixed, so lower speed does not obviously raise progress. Progress has stayed near 0.115 to 0.18 on the oval and 0.035 to 0.07 on the s-bend and slalom regardless of speed or gain. The off-track exit happens at a roughly fixed point on the course. Slowing the robot slows the time to that point but does not move the point, so the expected gain in progress is not shown. The draft's claim of 'progress above 0.2' would beat the best run so far (oval 0.176) and has no calculation behind it.

3) Iteration 7 is over-read as a clear signal. Its score fell from 39.8 (iterations 3, 5 and 6) to 36.7. Its metrics are mixed: oval progress fell from 0.1675 to 0.1151, s-bend progress fell from 0.0725 to 0.0406, and only slalom rose (0.0625 to 0.1125). Line-loss count also changed in a confounded way. Iterations 0, 1, 2 and 4 with different spans and speeds had 1 line-loss event, while 3, 5 and 6 had 2. Line loss tracks speed and gain as much as span, so the claim that narrowing the span 'reduces line losses' is not established. The draft keeps the geometry on the basis of this weak signal.

4) kd = 0.6 still produces a large sensor-edge kick. With 10 mm pitch and 0.25 weight steps, one edge crossing moves the signal by about 0.25 units. The derivative kick is about 0.25 x 100 x 0.6 = 15 turn units, roughly 5000 PWM counts, in a single 10 ms step. The draft's stated reason for lowering kd (to avoid amplifying edge transitions at the narrower span) is therefore only partly addressed. Steering_oscillation has been 0.06 to 0.18 in every run, so there is little evidence that kd damps anything. A kd of about 0.1 to 0.2 would be more defensible, or kd should be tested in isolation.

5) kp = 1.2 is a repeat of an earlier value. With the 0.25-per-sensor weight slope (about 25 per metre) times kp 1.2, the gain is about 30 turn units per metre. That is close to iteration 3 and iteration 6, which both failed at max_error 0.061 to 0.066. The draft gives no reason to expect a different outcome from those runs.

6) ki = 0.3 is not quantified. The integral is capped at plus or minus 2, so its maximum contribution is 0.6 turn units, about 210 PWM counts. The motor-mismatch bias is never estimated in metres or turn units, so 'fixed bias cancellation' cannot be checked against a 3 s run.

7) Stall and line-loss risk at 0.6 are low but not zero. Base PWM is about 30 percent, so the stall test (less than 0.002 progress in 50 steps) is unlikely to trigger on the development tracks. The 0.35 throttle during line loss becomes a larger share of forward motion at this speed, so recovery after any loss is slower. The draft does not mention this.",
    "rationale_critique": "1) The rationale claims the untested factor is speed, but speed was already varied from 0.8 to 1.6 with no change in outcome (see design point 1). The central logic of the draft is therefore wrong on its own evidence.

2) The expected results (max_error below about 0.05 m, progress above 0.2, line-loss events near 0 to 1) are stated as outcomes. None is derived from data, and the 0.05 m figure has no basis. Every design so far has produced max_error between 0.060 and 0.067. The rationale should label these as hypotheses.
